item.description:
Current time in
Manila6:07 p.m. Nov. 17
Latest
PinnedUpdated Nov. 17, 2026, 4:41 a.m. ET
David E. Sanger
Reporting from Manila
Here’s the latest.
President Trump on Tuesday began a whirlwind Asia trip in which he will meet Xi Jinping of China and other world leaders, with an unpredictable agenda that could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control and U.S. restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence chips.
Mr. Trump landed in Manila, where he is scheduled to meet with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines and attend a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders. After less than 24 hours there, he will head to the APEC economic summit in Shenzhen, China, where all eyes will be on his expected meeting with Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.
The brief itinerary appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.
Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind. Each leader will arrive at the session, planned for Thursday, with a different agenda, and some analysts have compared it to Yalta, where the leaders of the United States, Britain and the Soviet Union divided up postwar Europe in 1945.
That analogy has limits: No one thinks these three leaders, powerful as they are, are there to redefine the borders of any continent. But their very presence at one table would underscore they have major sway over the shape of the next world order. And for Mr. Trump, who loves the symbolism of a dramatic photo op, that may be enough.
On Tuesday, Mr. Trump will catch the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

item.title: [NYT World] These Ukrainians Aren’t in Combat. But They Deal With War Every Day.
item.description:
AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTYou have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load.
Mykhailo Biliak has spent most of his life in the funeral business, and he no longer remembers how many graves he has dug. But he knows he has buried more than 1,200 soldiers in Lviv, in western Ukraine, since Russia started its full-scale war in 2022. “The worst day was six funerals,” said Mr. Biliak, 62.
Hundreds of miles to the east, in a basement near the front line, Daryna Boiko, a 32-year-old anesthesiologist, prepared to attach an IV drip to a soldier wounded by a drone. “It won’t be scary,” she assured him. “It was scary out there,” he replied. “It’s fine here.”
In Kyiv, the capital, Hanna Buraho, a 53-year-old psychotherapist, made tea after a session with a group of soldiers. More than 5,000 service members have been through her rehabilitation program, which uses horses. “When the war started, everyone rushed to help each other, and every person wanted to do something of their own, so this is my contribution,” Ms. Buraho said.
This Ukrainian doctor works near the front, trying to save wounded soldiers.
This man has buried more than 1,200 soldiers.
This therapist tries to help damaged veterans heal.
This forensic pathologist once helped to solve crimes. Now he identifies fallen soldiers.
In Odesa, in southern Ukraine, two morgue workers pushed open the heavy, rusted doors of a refrigerated rail carriage that contained the remains of dozens of soldiers killed in battle. A white bag was placed on an autopsy table, and Ruslan Fedorenko, 61, a forensic pathologist, turned to his work.
None of these people carry weapons. But like Ukrainians across the country, they deal with the war and its consequences every day.

This class in conduit bending at The Electrical Trades Center of Central Ohio is part of an apprenticeship program Baukman began in the spring. She's here in class one day out of every two weeks. Other days, she's out on construction sites, working under the supervision of journeymen electricians.

The coastal town of Sonderborg in southern Denmark hosts two biogas facilities converting livestock slurry, food waste and crop residues into enough biogas to meet 100 percent of the surrounding region’s annual gas demand [Courtesy ProjectZero]By Nick ClarkPublished On 17 Nov 202617 Nov 2026
As the world seeks to cut carbon emissions to slow global warming, livestock manure is driving Denmark’s energy transition.
Pigs are big business in the Scandinavian nation, accounting for a quarter of its food exports. There are as many as 12 million breeding pigs in the country at any one time – more than double the human population, and that ratio spirals if you account for 30 million more produced for slaughter and live export every year.
Managing pig and cattle waste has long been a significant challenge. According to the Danish Agriculture and Food Council, Denmark’s pig sector annually produces more than 17 million tonnes of manure, mostly liquid slurry, emitting considerable amounts of greenhouse gas in the form of methane and nitrous oxide.
However, Denmark has been engineering a biogas boom, developing facilities to convert livestock waste into renewable natural gas to power the national grid and transport, fuel homes and make fertiliser.
In just more than a decade, the country has upscaled a handful of small biogas operations into about 150 industrial-sized plants, with up to 70 percent of the processed raw materials coming from pig and cattle manure.
Today, Denmark has Europe’s highest share of biogas in its gas grid, at about 40 percent. And this has timely benefits, given the volatile oil and gas markets caused by the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran.

item.description:
President Trump arrived in the Philippines Tuesday to start a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit later this week.
Ahead of his departure from Washington Monday, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China.
President Trump waves American and Philippine flags after he arrived at Ninoy Aquino International Airport on Nov. 17, 2026 to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila.
Eloisa Lopez / POOL / AFP via Getty Images
The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first among the three leaders, is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.
Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.
In Manila, the president will attend the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. He will meet with leaders of Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.
On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. item.title: [NYT World] Carney and Xi Announce Canada-China Trade Pact
item.description:
AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTYou have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load.
Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, have struck an agreement to reduce some tariffs between their countries, a largely symbolic move that shows relations between the two countries are warming as Canada’s ties to the United States falter.
While the expanded trade between China and Canada resulting from the accord in the Chinese tech and financial hub Shenzhen will be modest, involving just $280 million in exports, the pact — as well as the seemingly amicable meeting — illustrates a contrast to Mr. Carney’s relationship with President Trump. Earlier this year, Mr. Carney said that the United States was “at war” with Canada after trade negotiations between the two countries collapsed in acrimony.
Talks are restarting between Canada and the United States but there is no indication that Washington will back away from key irritants including tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian autos, steel and aluminum.
Since entering politics last year, Mr. Carney has been traveling the world to diversify Canada’s economic and political ties away from the United States. Those efforts include current talks to make Canada the European Union’s first associate member and Mr. Carney’s second formal meeting this year with Mr. Xi.
“The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems,” Mr. Carney said at the start of the meeting with Mr. Xi on Tuesday.
He added that Canada is ahead of schedule with its goal of a 50 percent increase in exports to China by the end of the decade.

item.description:
Image caption,
Images circulated on social media appeared to show part of the road section of the Crimea bridge has collapsedByOlivia Ireland and Sarah Rainsford, Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent, KyivPublished17 November 2026, 03:46 GMTUpdated 40 minutes ago
A key bridge linking occupied Crimea and Russia is closed after a Ukrainian strike inflicted major damage on the prized Kremlin asset.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials showed a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - had collapsed into the water.
Russian officials confirmed the structure had been damaged by drones, while Russia's deputy prime minister was due to chair an emergency meeting to discuss the situation.
Meanwhile, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.
Former Ukrainian adviser Anton Gerashchenko shared images and video footage appearing to show extensive damage to the road section of the Crimea bridge, with remnants of the support arch and road section seen protruding from the water below.
The bridge, which has come under repeated attack by Ukrainian forces, was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2018.
While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the Crimea bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.
The timing of the Crimea bridge strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This strike could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
While the long-term impact of the strike on was not immediately clear, the bridge has been used to move troops and supplies into Crimea and towards the front line.

Tokyo protests after two suspected Russian aircraft violate Japanese airspace
Japan said it has protested to Moscow after two suspected Russian warplanes temporarily entered Japanese airspace off the country’s southwestern coast on Tuesday as tensions escalate between the two sidesByMARI YAMAGUCHI Associated PressNovember 17, 2026, 1:18 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
TOKYO -- Japan said it strongly protested to Moscow on Tuesday after two suspected Russian aircraft entered its airspace off its southwestern coast, the latest incident fueling escalating tensions between the neighbors.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told reporters the suspected Russian aircraft early Tuesday violated Japanese airspace for about five minutes near Fukuoka, long enough for the Air Self-Defense Force to scramble fighter jets and send warnings.
Japan's government has lodged "an extremely stern protest" and “strongly” demanded preventive measures be taken, Koizumi said. He did not specify the types of aircraft involved.
“The violation of the Japanese airspace by the Russian aircraft is not only a serious violation of our country's sovereignty, but also a threat to our safety,” Koizumi said. “It is absolutely unacceptable.”
The Russian aircraft flew across the Tsushima Strait, then headed south and flew above the waters between Taiwan and Japan's westernmost island of Yonaguni, Koizumi said.
Separately, South Korea’s military said several Russian military aircraft temporarily entered the country’s air defense identification zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan on Monday, though they did not violate South Korean airspace.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said the military had detected the aircraft before they entered the zone and scrambled fighter jets. The South’s military did not disclose the number of Russian aircraft it detected or what types of planes they were.

item.description:
Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty ImagesByMerlyn Thomas, BBC Verify correspondent and Paul Brown, BBC VerifyPublished4 hours ago
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.
Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.
Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there were multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.
The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.
With the DSNS saying the death toll had risen to at least 72 people, the attack on Komyshuvakha has become the second deadliest single incident of the Ukraine war.
Image source, DSNSImage caption,
Emergency service vehicles have also been targeted
Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".
He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.

item.title: [CBS News World] Protests flare in Philippines over Trump's visit and planned AI hub
item.description:
Manila, Philippines — Protests against President Trump's visit to the Philippines have popped up around the country, as local residents criticize a Trump administration project to build an artificial intelligence and manufacturing hub just north of the country's capital of Manila.
In the opening salvo for Pax Silica, a U.S. State Department-led international initiative to secure non-Chinese supply chains for high-tech manufacturing, a more than 4,000-acre manufacturing hub is planned to be built in the Philippines.
Protesters in Manila on Monday held signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or a devil, and signs calling on the public to reject the Pax Silica initiative.
Critics argue the proposed industrial hub will displace farming communities and the Indigenous Aeta tribe, harm the country's water supply and represent U.S. imperialism over the Philippines.
"They have been grabbing our lands. They have been grabbing our economy. … Pax Silica is just for the U.S. It's not for us," said Maninging Vilog, a teacher and advocate for Aeta communities.
"If you look at the farmers, what do they care about AI? The people selling water … selling cigarettes, the people who drive buses. What do they care about AI?" said Kaiser Cortina, a 20-year-old protester.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., also a subject of the protests this week, supports the hub. He said in October he is "terribly excited" about the project's economic benefits, framing it as a "grand opportunity" for the country to move up the "value chain" by shifting into advanced manufacturing and research, according to PhilStar Global.
Marcos' administration has claimed the project could create 100,000 to 130,000 jobs.

item.title: [BBC World] Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Pakistan's ex-PM says doctors have warned that he is "highly vulnerable to ⁠a brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest"ByCaroline Davies, Pakistan correspondent and Kelly NgPublished8 hours ago
Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating.
"At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive," the cricket star-turned-politician wrote in a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar.
Authorities in Islamabad maintain that Khan gets seen weekly by doctors, who have assessed that he is of "satisfactory" health.
Khan, who faces more than 100 charges, has been in prison since August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Khan argues the cases against them, ranging from corruption to selling state gifts, are politically motivated.
Concerns over Khan's health have grown louder in the past year, with his family claiming he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
In his letter, Khan wrote that doctors have told him he is "highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest", and that his heart has already "suffered damage".
He also expressed concern for Bushra Bibi, whom he says suffered a detached retina in April and underwent surgery in secrecy. Khan said he fears she may lose her sight without further surgery.
"I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice," he wrote.
He said that he is being held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day, where he is allowed neither visits by his family nor access to books and television, and that this has "taken a heavy toll" on his mental health.

Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

The meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said.
The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, the first of their kind, will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and cement Xi’s status as a global power broker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he would be speaking to his Chinese and Russian counterparts about denuclearisation, the war in Iran, economics, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”. US officials had earlier indicated that Trump would not discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine during the trip.
Trump also said he may meet North Korea’s Kim Jong-un in what would be their first meeting of his second term. “We may meet with Kim Jong-un also,” Trump said. “So that will be good … we have a chance to accomplish a lot.”

Pope Leo XIV has bid farewell to his beloved homeland of PeruByNICOLE WINFIELD Associated Press, ASTRID SUÁREZ Associated Press, and LUIS ANDRES HENAO Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 9:43 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
LIMA, Peru -- LIMA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV bid farewell to his beloved second homeland of Peru on Monday with an “hasta luego,” after a marathon 12-day South American tour that tested his stamina after lung cancer surgery.
During the traditional popemobile ride before Leo's final Mass, someone threw an apparent rosary toward the pope that seemed to hit him in the face. The pope winced and touched his temple, but he proceeded on and the Mass began as planned. The Vatican said some 1.5 million people attended.
The faithful often toss rosaries, stuffed animals, sports jerseys and other items towards the popemobile and Leo has often wowed the crowd with his quick reflexes in catching them. His bodyguards, though, have lamented that such tossed objects are among their chief concerns in protecting the pope when he is out in public.
For the Chicago-born Leo, who spent two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop, the trip was an emotional homecoming to a place that he has credited with teaching him how to be a shepherd. Upon arrival, he declared that Peru was his “patria” or homeland, and he sang the national anthem alongside President Keiko Fujimori. Leo has American and Peruvian citizenship.
“It was here that you taught me how to be a bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter,” Leo said at the end of Mass.
Over the course of the trip, it became clear that Leo modeled his ministry in Peru and now for the universal Catholic Church on the figure of the first archbishop of Lima, St. Turibius of Mogrovejo.

An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack has thanked well-wishers around the worldByROD MCGUIRK Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 1:18 AM
MELBOURNE, Australia -- An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack thanked well-wishers around the world Monday and revealed she had been discharged from a hospital where she spent the past month.
In her first public statement since being struck by a SUV on Oct. 19, Helen Haines said she was “very pleased to confirm” she had left Melbourne’s The Alfred hospital.
Witnesses said she was repeatedly rammed by the vehicle outside her electorate office.
The 65-year-old independent lawmaker said she would remain in Melbourne for the “rehabilitation stage” of her recovery. Her staff would not disclose where her rehabilitation would take place for privacy reasons.
“This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage,” Haines said.
“I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across (my electorate) Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing,” she added.
Haines was in critical condition hours after she was struck when she was flown to Melbourne by helicopter from her hometown of Wangaratta, 236 kilometers (147 miles) to the northeast.
Surgeons amputated both her legs within a few days.
The hospital listed her as critical until Oct. 24 when her condition was downgraded to serious but stable. She had been listed as stable since Nov. 6.

One of the AI industry's most important figures has resigned amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs with two women - one a suspected Chinese spy and the other a company executive.
Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset.
Now he has resigned after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair.

How was Huang removed?
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company.
It had 11 directors on its board, including Huang. The firm's CEO could be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors.

It thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions" to Nvidia, which it said were "profound".
There was no mention of the accusations of adultery.

Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO.

Watch: Chris Cash says counter-terror officers entered his bedroom and arrested himByJoe Pike, politics investigations correspondent and Phil Kemp, politics reporterPublished11 November 2026
A British man who was charged with spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map".
Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister.
The messages show how Cash's friend in China, Chris Berry - with whom he had been sharing information - dramatically described a "secret" meeting between Berry and a high-ranking Chinese official.
Berry said he had been told that China was concerned about how a British MP it had sanctioned might be promoted to a cabinet role.
The messages also reveal how Cash used his friend as a reference during vetting for a parliamentary pass - which was approved.
Like Cash, Berry was also charged with espionage. The two men consistently maintained their innocence.
In Cash's first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", he says he would "never do anything" to harm UK national security.
But he admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, whom he met in 2018 when they both taught English in a school in China.
Although the trove of messages shows him discussing sensitive topics, there is no evidence in them that Cash was paid by, or sympathetic to, the Chinese Communist Party.
